# **Advanced Architecture Design for Domain-Invariant Aquaculture Pond Identification**

## **I. Challenge Protocol and the Physical Data Trap**

The task of identifying aquaculture ponds from isolated ![][image1] patches using satellite image time series (SITS) presents extraordinary combinatorial and optimization challenges. The fundamental complexity arises from severe covariate shifts, sensor asymmetry, and rigid evaluation metrics imposed by the competition framework. The binary classification problem mandates that predictions be evaluated strictly at a hardcoded 0.5 probability threshold using a composite metric of ![][image2]. Because post-hoc threshold tuning is forbidden, the network's output logits must perfectly align with the true posterior distribution of the target domain.  
An analysis of the dataset reveals structural anomalies that induce catastrophic overfitting in standard high-capacity architectures. The organizers' decision to resolve a prior target-sorting leak by merging the original hidden test set with the training set (yielding 1,817 unique spatial locations post-deduplication) successfully eliminated spatial coordinate exploits but established an intensely adversarial relationship between the training and test distributions. The public training data exposes a fully observed 12-month temporal sequence of Sentinel-1 active radar and Sentinel-2 passive optical composites. Conversely, the 1,030 test samples simulate real-world observation constraints, artificially masking the time series to reveal only consecutive blocks of 4, 5, or 6 months, replacing the remaining periods with a \-9999 placeholder.  
Compounding this temporal shift is a critical physical sensor asymmetry driven by regional climatology. Sentinel-2 multispectral sensors operate passively and are entirely blind to the earth's surface when obstructed by monsoon cloud cover. This results in massive, localized data dropouts heavily concentrated in the months of June (7.3% of test rows) and October (17.6% of test rows). In approximately 2.6% of the test entries, the optical bands are entirely masked, yet the Sentinel-1 C-band active synthetic aperture radar (VH, VV backscatter) remains fully populated due to its ability to penetrate cloud droplets and precipitation. Consequently, models that rely on standard sequence imputation or simplistic mean-pooling across the 24 input channels systematically collapse under the extreme variance of the missing optical signatures.  
The current baseline framework—a temporal Transformer trained from scratch utilizing left-aligned relative time coordinates—achieves a public leaderboard score of 0.8955. However, highly expressive Transformer models naturally act as high-capacity unconstrained sequence learners. They tend to memorize regional spectral-temporal signatures rather than learning the physical invariants of standing water. When subjected to the adversarial covariate shift between the fully observed training sequences and the heavily masked test sequences, performance degrades sharply. Established mitigation strategies, such as amplitude-level normalization (detrending), the injection of pretrained zero-shot geospatial foundation models, and label-shift loss weighting during training, have universally failed. Amplitude detrending destroys the absolute low-backscatter physical signature required by C-band radar to identify specular reflection over standing water. Furthermore, standard loss re-weighting approaches collapse the effective sample size without resolving the underlying domain discrepancy.  
To bridge the performance gap toward the targeted 0.945+ threshold, the architecture must transition from a capacity-heavy memorization engine into a domain-invariant, physics-constrained pipeline. The following sections provide a mathematically rigorous and technically exhaustive blueprint for four critical advancement vectors: prior-shift adaptation via maximum likelihood, unsupervised temporal representation alignment, low-capacity inductive biases through alternative model classes, and capacity-neutral physical feature reframing.

## **II. Prior-Shift Adaptation via Saerens Expectation-Maximization**

The divergence in class prevalence between the training set (approximately 40% positive) and the hidden test set creates an extreme prior probability shift, also formally known as label shift. Under label shift, the marginal probability of observing a particular class changes between the training and test distributions (![][image3]), while the conditional probability of the features given the label remains constant (![][image4])1. Because the challenge strictly enforces a 0.5 classification threshold for the F1-score evaluation, posterior probabilities emitted by the network must be perfectly calibrated to the target domain's unobserved prior; otherwise, the rigid decision boundary will produce massive false positive or false negative clusters4.  
If the base classifier outputs a posterior ![][image5] trained on a source prior ![][image6], these probabilities will fundamentally misrepresent the optimal decision boundary in the target domain3. The Maximum Likelihood Label Shift (MLLS) algorithm, originally formulated as the Saerens Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, provides a mathematically optimal, unsupervised mechanism to estimate the target prior and recalibrate network predictions without requiring labeled target data1.

### **Mathematical Formulation of Maximum Likelihood Label Shift (MLLS)**

The MLLS algorithm operates under the assumption of anti-causal learning, which is highly appropriate for remote sensing classification where the physical land cover (the label ![][image7]) causes the observed spectral signatures (the features ![][image8])2.

| Label Shift Adaptation Method | Underlying Mechanism | Assumption Requirements | Performance with Neural Networks |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Black Box Shift Estimation (BBSE)** | Moment-matching based on confusion matrices. | Invertible confusion matrix; does not require perfect calibration. | Suboptimal when confusion matrices are volatile under small sample sizes1. |
| **Regularized Learning under Label Shift (RLLS)** | Moment-matching with regularization to prevent extreme shifts. | Similar to BBSE. | Outperforms BBSE but generally inferior to EM when models are calibrated1. |
| **Saerens Expectation-Maximization (MLLS)** | Iterative maximum likelihood estimation of target prior via Bayes' rule. | Requires calibrated posterior probabilities from the source classifier. | State-of-the-art when combined with bias-corrected temperature scaling or sigmoid output calibration1. |

The EM procedure iteratively estimates the target prior ![][image9] and updates the target posteriors ![][image10] by treating the unknown test labels as latent variables1.

> 1. **Initialization**: The algorithm initializes the target prior estimate ![][image11] using the empirical source prior ![][image6] derived from the training set.  
> 2. **Expectation Step (E-step)**: For each test sample ![][image12], the target posterior is updated using the current prior estimate. Let ![][image13] be the output probability of the calibrated neural network on the source domain. By applying Bayes' theorem and the label shift assumption, the posterior at iteration ![][image14] is1:  
>    ![][image15]  
> 3. **Maximization Step (M-step)**: The target prior is updated by taking the mathematical expectation of the newly estimated posteriors across all ![][image16] unlabeled test samples4:  
>    ![][image17]

The algorithm iterates until the absolute difference ![][image18] falls below a defined convergence threshold5. Once convergence is achieved, the network's raw logits can be monotonically shifted. The optimal logit adjustment required to mathematically align the decision boundary to the hardcoded 0.5 threshold is derived from the log-odds ratio of the estimated test prior to the train prior.

### **PyTorch Implementation: Saerens EM Calibration**

The following module implements the MLLS calibration sequence. It is designed to be executed strictly as an unsupervised post-processing step on the test logits, ensuring no data leakage occurs during the training phase.

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

class SaerensLabelShift(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Implements the Saerens Expectation-Maximization (MLLS) algorithm   
    for unsupervised prior shift adaptation under rigid threshold constraints.  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, train\_prior: float, max\_iter: int \= 1000, tol: float \= 1e-6):  
        """  
        Args:  
            train\_prior: Empirical probability of the positive class in the training set.  
            max\_iter: Maximum number of EM iterations.  
            tol: Convergence tolerance for the prior estimate.  
        """  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.train\_prior \= torch.tensor(train\_prior, dtype=torch.float32)  
        self.max\_iter \= max\_iter  
        self.tol \= tol

    def fit\_transform(self, test\_logits: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        """  
        Estimates the target prior via EM and applies a monotonic logit shift.  
          
        Args:  
            test\_logits: Raw logit predictions (1D tensor) from the base model.  
              
        Returns:  
            calibrated\_logits: Logits adjusted for the estimated target prior.  
            q\_prior: The final estimated target prior probability.  
        """  
        device \= test\_logits.device  
        train\_p \= self.train\_prior.to(device)  
          
        \# Source posteriors f(y=1|x\_i)  
        source\_probs \= torch.sigmoid(test\_logits)  
          
        \# Initialize target prior q(y=1) with train prior p(y=1)  
        q\_prior \= train\_p.clone()  
          
        for step in range(self.max\_iter):  
            \# Expectation Step: Calculate q^{(k)}(y=1|x\_i)  
            \# Utilizing the label shift likelihood ratio  
            num \= (q\_prior / train\_p) \* source\_probs  
            den \= num \+ ((1.0 \- q\_prior) / (1.0 \- train\_p)) \* (1.0 \- source\_probs)  
              
            \# Add epsilon to prevent division by zero in extreme confidence cases  
            q\_posterior \= num / (den \+ 1e-9)  
              
            \# Maximization Step: Update q^{(k+1)}(y=1)  
            q\_prior\_new \= q\_posterior.mean()  
              
            \# Convergence check  
            if torch.abs(q\_prior\_new \- q\_prior) \< self.tol:  
                q\_prior \= q\_prior\_new  
                break  
                  
            q\_prior \= q\_prior\_new

        \# Calculate the mathematically optimal logit shift  
        \# logit\_shift \= log(Odds\_target) \- log(Odds\_source)  
        odds\_target \= q\_prior / (1.0 \- q\_prior \+ 1e-9)  
        odds\_source \= train\_p / (1.0 \- train\_p \+ 1e-9)  
          
        logit\_shift \= torch.log(odds\_target) \- torch.log(odds\_source)  
          
        \# Apply the mathematically optimal monotonic shift to the logits  
        calibrated\_logits \= test\_logits \+ logit\_shift  
        return calibrated\_logits, q\_prior

This procedure mathematically guarantees that the threshold mapping evaluated by the competition backend natively aligns with the empirical test prior. Crucially, because a monotonic logit shift preserves the rank order of the predictions, it optimizes the 0.6 F1-Score metric without degrading the 0.4 ROC-AUC metric evaluation, fully satisfying the TargetRAUC submission constraint.

## **III. Temporal Representation Alignment and Test-Time Adaptation**

Standard supervised training paradigms collapse when the test distribution contains adversarial masking and phenologically shifted observation windows. To prevent the Transformer's latent space from over-mapping to the contiguous 12-month training domain, unsupervised temporal representation alignment techniques must be integrated during the training phase, subsequently supplemented by Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) during inference7.

### **Transductive Alignment via TimeMatch and Match-And-Deform (MAD)**

Cross-domain transfer in satellite image time series (SITS) is notoriously disrupted by temporal shifts10. Crops and aquaculture ponds in different spatial regions exhibit similar overall patterns, but the timing of these signatures shifts along the temporal axis10.  
The TimeMatch framework addresses this explicitly by attempting to estimate the unsupervised temporal offset between the target and source regions10. TimeMatch operates iteratively: it extracts softmax predictions from a source-trained model across various simulated temporal shifts of the target data10. It then selects the shift that maximizes prediction confidence across a diverse set of classes, using this estimated shift to generate high-accuracy pseudo-labels for self-training on the target domain10.  
Alternatively, the Match-And-Deform (MAD) approach formulates temporal adaptation as a dual optimization problem, blending Optimal Transport (OT) with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW)14. MAD seeks to find a coupling matrix ![][image19] that aligns the feature distribution between the source and target domains using an optimal transport loss, while simultaneously allowing non-linear temporal distortions across the chronologies utilizing DTW14. The MAD loss directly measures the dissimilarity between domains up to a global temporal alignment, enforcing a domain-invariant latent representation within deep neural networks15.

| Alignment Technique | Core Mathematical Mechanism | Application Phase | Computational Complexity |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **TimeMatch** | Iterative temporal shift estimation and pseudo-label generation. | Post-training / Self-training | Moderate (requires iterative inference). |
| **Match-And-Deform (MAD)** | Optimal Transport (OT) coupling combined with Dynamic Time Warping (DTW). | In-training loss | Extremely High (![][image20] for pure OT). |
| **Deep CORAL** | Covariance matrix alignment (second-order statistics) via Frobenius norm. | In-training loss | Low (![][image21] for feature dimension ![][image22]). |

While MAD is theoretically profound, pure Optimal Transport calculations suffer from severe computational bottlenecks, rendering them prohibitive for rapid batch-wise gradient descent in high-frequency competition environments. A highly effective, computationally stable alternative for representation alignment is Correlation Alignment (CORAL), a form of Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) that aligns the second-order statistics of the latent features between domains18.

### **Feature Alignment via Deep CORAL**

Deep CORAL minimizes the distance between the covariance matrices of the source and target representations extracted from the Transformer's projection layer18. By constraining the covariance, the model is mathematically forced to learn a feature representation that is invariant to the temporal masking distribution of the test set, preventing the network from relying on features that only exist in the fully-observed source domain19.  
Let ![][image23] and ![][image24] be the source and target feature batches of dimension ![][image22]. The covariance matrices ![][image25] and ![][image26] are computed, and the CORAL loss is defined as the squared Frobenius norm of their difference18:  
$$ \\mathcal{L}\_{CORAL} \= \\frac{1}{4d^2} \\vert{} \\vert{} C\_S \- C\_T \\vert{}\\vert{}\_F^2 $$

### **Unsupervised Test-Time Adaptation (TTA)**

To finalize the reality gap closure, Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) dynamically adjusts a subset of the model's parameters directly on the unlabeled test data immediately prior to inference9. Following the principles established by TENT (Test Entropy Minimization) and SHOT (Source Hypothesis Transfer), the adaptation protocol optimizes the affine transformations of the projection layer (or normalization layers) to minimize the Shannon entropy of the test predictions7. By enforcing high-confidence predictions on the target data, TTA aligns the learned boundaries to the target manifold without requiring access to the original source training data23.

### **PyTorch Implementation: CORAL Loss and TENT Wrapper**

The integration of CORAL into the training loop and a TENT-based wrapper during inference provides robust transductive alignment.

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn

def compute\_covariance(features: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
    """  
    Computes the covariance matrix of a batch of latent features.  
      
    Args:  
        features: Tensor of shape (batch\_size, d\_model)  
    Returns:  
        cov: Covariance matrix of shape (d\_model, d\_model)  
    """  
    n \= features.size(0)  
    \# Mean centering  
    mean \= torch.mean(features, dim=0, keepdim=True)  
    features\_centered \= features \- mean  
      
    \# Covariance matrix calculation  
    cov \= torch.mm(features\_centered.t(), features\_centered) / (n \- 1 \+ 1e-9)  
    return cov

class CORALLoss(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Computes the CORrelation ALignment (CORAL) loss to minimize covariate shift.  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()

    def forward(self, source\_features: torch.Tensor, target\_features: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        d \= source\_features.size(1)  
        cov\_source \= compute\_covariance(source\_features)  
        cov\_target \= compute\_covariance(target\_features)  
          
        \# Squared Frobenius norm of the difference  
        diff \= cov\_source \- cov\_target  
        loss \= torch.norm(diff, p='fro')\*\*2 / (4.0 \* d \* d)  
        return loss

class TTAModelAdapter(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Test-Time Adaptation wrapper utilizing Entropy Minimization (TENT framework).  
    Adapts projection/normalization parameters to the unlabeled test batch.  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, model: nn.Module, lr: float \= 1e-4, steps: int \= 3):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.model \= model  
        self.steps \= steps  
          
        \# Isolate parameters for adaptation to prevent catastrophic forgetting  
        self.adaptable\_params \= \[\]  
        for name, param in self.model.named\_parameters():  
            if 'projection' in name or 'norm' in name:  
                param.requires\_grad \= True  
                self.adaptable\_params.append(param)  
            else:  
                param.requires\_grad \= False  
                  
        self.optimizer \= torch.optim.Adam(self.adaptable\_params, lr=lr)

    def forward(self, x\_test: torch.Tensor, mask\_test: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# Enable training mode for adaptation parameters  
        self.model.train()  
          
        for \_ in range(self.steps):  
            self.optimizer.zero\_grad()  
            logits \= self.model(x\_test, mask\_test)  
            probs \= torch.sigmoid(logits)  
              
            \# Shannon Entropy minimization for binary classification  
            entropy \= \- (probs \* torch.log(probs \+ 1e-9) \+   
                         (1.0 \- probs) \* torch.log(1.0 \- probs \+ 1e-9))  
            loss \= entropy.mean()  
            loss.backward()  
            self.optimizer.step()  
              
        \# Switch back to evaluation mode for final deterministic inference  
        self.model.eval()  
        with torch.no\_grad():  
            final\_logits \= self.model(x\_test, mask\_test)  
              
        return final\_logits

## **IV. Set Transformers and Order Invariance**

The baseline temporal Transformer leverages relative left-aligned positional encodings. While this neutralizes explicit calendar-month memorization, the rigid sequential framework inherently forces the model to assume uniform chronological progression. When confronted with heavily masked sequences and extreme phenological variance across geographic locations, rigid chronologies degrade inference capabilities26.

### **Duration-Normalized Positional Encodings**

To introduce temporal elasticity, Duration-Normalized Positional Encodings map discrete timestep indices into a continuous fractional space27. If an observed window spans ![][image27] active months (excluding the \-9999 dropouts), the step position ![][image28] within that active window is mapped as:  
![][image29]  
This mathematically normalizes the duration constraint, ensuring that the model processes the sequence based on its proportional internal progress rather than rigid absolute or relative monthly indices27.

### **Permutation-Invariant Set Transformers**

An alternative, and arguably superior, paradigm under severe masking is to abandon positional encodings entirely. Since identifying a managed aquaculture pond relies on detecting specific, highly persistent structural states—such as persistently low backscatter or sustained water indices over an extended duration—the exact temporal sequence is less critical than the sheer existence and ratio of these physical states across the valid observations29.  
By treating the valid months as an unordered "Set" of physical observations, the architecture becomes immune to permutation and missing temporal steps. The Set Transformer architecture provides a mathematically proven, permutation-invariant framework for modeling interactions among elements in a set29.  
Standard self-attention mechanisms scale quadratically ![][image30], which is inefficient for subset processing. The Set Transformer mitigates this by utilizing an Induced Set Attention Block (ISAB)33. ISAB introduces ![][image16] learnable inducing points to compress the input set ![][image31] into an intermediate representation ![][image32], effectively reducing attention complexity to ![][image33]35. Following the encoder blocks, the representation is pooled using Pooling by Multihead Attention (PMA), which applies cross-attention using a single trainable query vector (or multiple seed vectors) to compress the variable-length set into a fixed-size invariant feature vector32.  
A known vulnerability of permutation-invariant neural networks, including Set Transformers, is their susceptibility to vanishing or exploding gradients when stacked deeply30. To counteract this, careful application of layer normalization and the "clean path principle" for residual connections must be maintained30.

### **PyTorch Implementation: Set Transformer Components (ISAB & PMA)**

The following implementation defines the core permutation-invariant modules that can entirely replace the standard sequential Transformer encoder.

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  
import torch.nn.functional as F  
import math

class MAB(nn.Module):  
    """ Multihead Attention Block """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, dim\_Q: int, dim\_K: int, dim\_V: int, num\_heads: int, ln: bool \= True):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.dim\_V \= dim\_V  
        self.num\_heads \= num\_heads  
        self.fc\_q \= nn.Linear(dim\_Q, dim\_V)  
        self.fc\_k \= nn.Linear(dim\_K, dim\_V)  
        self.fc\_v \= nn.Linear(dim\_K, dim\_V)  
        self.fc\_o \= nn.Linear(dim\_V, dim\_V)  
        self.ln0 \= nn.LayerNorm(dim\_V) if ln else nn.Identity()  
        self.ln1 \= nn.LayerNorm(dim\_V) if ln else nn.Identity()

    def forward(self, Q: torch.Tensor, K: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor \= None) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        Q\_proj \= self.fc\_q(Q)  
        K\_proj \= self.fc\_k(K)  
        V\_proj \= self.fc\_v(K)

        dim\_split \= self.dim\_V // self.num\_heads  
        Q\_split \= Q\_proj.view(Q.shape\[0\], Q.shape\[1\], self.num\_heads, dim\_split).transpose(1, 2)  
        K\_split \= K\_proj.view(K.shape\[0\], K.shape\[1\], self.num\_heads, dim\_split).transpose(1, 2)  
        V\_split \= V\_proj.view(K.shape\[0\], K.shape\[1\], self.num\_heads, dim\_split).transpose(1, 2)

        scores \= torch.matmul(Q\_split, K\_split.transpose(2, 3)) / math.sqrt(dim\_split)  
          
        if mask is not None:  
            \# mask shape: (batch, 1, 1, seq\_len)  
            scores \= scores.masked\_fill(mask \== 0, \-1e9)  
              
        A \= torch.softmax(scores, dim=-1)  
        O \= torch.matmul(A, V\_split)  
        O \= O.transpose(1, 2).contiguous().view(Q.shape\[0\], Q.shape\[1\], self.dim\_V)  
          
        \# Clean path residual connections to prevent gradient vanishing  
        O \= self.ln0(Q\_proj \+ O)  
        O \= self.ln1(O \+ F.relu(self.fc\_o(O)))  
        return O

class ISAB(nn.Module):  
    """ Induced Set Attention Block to reduce computational complexity """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, dim\_in: int, dim\_out: int, num\_heads: int, num\_inds: int, ln: bool \= True):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.I \= nn.Parameter(torch.Tensor(1, num\_inds, dim\_out))  
        nn.init.xavier\_uniform\_(self.I)  
        self.mab0 \= MAB(dim\_out, dim\_in, dim\_out, num\_heads, ln=ln)  
        self.mab1 \= MAB(dim\_in, dim\_out, dim\_out, num\_heads, ln=ln)

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor \= None) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        \# Inducing points attend to the input set  
        H \= self.mab0(self.I.repeat(X.size(0), 1, 1), X, mask)  
        \# Input set attends to the inducing points  
        return self.mab1(X, H)

class PMA(nn.Module):  
    """ Pooling by Multihead Attention """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, dim: int, num\_heads: int, num\_seeds: int, ln: bool \= True):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
        self.S \= nn.Parameter(torch.Tensor(1, num\_seeds, dim))  
        nn.init.xavier\_uniform\_(self.S)  
        self.mab \= MAB(dim, dim, dim, num\_heads, ln=ln)

    def forward(self, X: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor \= None) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        return self.mab(self.S.repeat(X.size(0), 1, 1), X, mask)

## **V. Low-Capacity Inductive Biases via Spectral-Temporal Convolutions**

While Set Transformers and standard self-attention models excel in high-capacity sequence mapping, their extreme expressiveness makes them notoriously susceptible to memorizing confounding environmental noise and regional correlations26. To achieve robust generalization under massive domain shifts, it is highly advantageous to engineer an ensemble component built upon strong inductive biases, forcing the network to extract localized physical signatures rather than global chronological patterns26.

### **CropNet: Joint Spectral-Temporal CNN**

The CropNet architecture abandons full-sequence self-attention in favor of lightweight temporal convolutions26. By applying convolutions directly across the temporal axis, CropNet acts as a low-capacity feature extractor that intrinsically limits the receptive field26.

| Architecture Type | Inductive Bias | Receptive Field | Vulnerability to Covariate Shift |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Temporal Transformer** | Minimal (fully connected attention) | Global (all tokens attend to all tokens) | High (Prone to memorizing sequence length and regional artifacts)26. |
| **Set Transformer** | Permutation Invariance | Global (set-wide interactions) | Moderate (Protects against temporal shifts, but can overfit to spectral noise)30. |
| **CropNet (1D/2D CNN)** | Local translation invariance | Localized (constrained by kernel size) | Low (Extracts invariant structural transitions, highly robust to geography)26. |

This structural convolutional constraint prevents the network from learning spurious chronological relationships spanning across the entire 12-month period. Instead, it prioritizes the localized extraction of invariant signatures, such as the rapid spectral transition of a dry field being flooded into an inundated aquaculture pond26. CropNet achieves superior geographic generalizability by applying sequential 1D convolutions that map raw spectral bands into temporal activation maps, drastically reducing parameter counts while maintaining high spatial resilience26.

### **PyTorch Implementation: Temporal CropNet Backbone**

The following implementation provides a 1D temporal convolutional backbone designed to serve as a low-capacity alternative. It natively supports sequence masking by enforcing explicit zero-padding on missing timesteps to prevent noise contamination across the convolutional receptive field.

Python  
import torch  
import torch.nn as nn  
import torch.nn.functional as F

class CropNetTemporalBackbone(nn.Module):  
    """  
    Lightweight Temporal Convolutional Network (CropNet) for extracting  
    invariant spectral-temporal signatures with strong inductive biases.  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, in\_channels: int, out\_dim: int \= 64, dropout: float \= 0.3):  
        super().\_\_init\_\_()  
          
        \# Temporal convolutions acting over the 12-month sequence length  
        \# in\_channels: 24 (12 raw bands \+ 12 binary missing indicators)  
        self.conv1 \= nn.Conv1d(in\_channels=in\_channels, out\_channels=32, kernel\_size=3, padding=1)  
        self.bn1 \= nn.BatchNorm1d(32)  
          
        self.conv2 \= nn.Conv1d(in\_channels=32, out\_channels=64, kernel\_size=3, padding=1)  
        self.bn2 \= nn.BatchNorm1d(64)  
          
        self.conv3 \= nn.Conv1d(in\_channels=64, out\_channels=128, kernel\_size=3, padding=1)  
        self.bn3 \= nn.BatchNorm1d(128)  
          
        self.dropout \= nn.Dropout(dropout)  
        self.fc \= nn.Linear(128, out\_dim)

    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, mask: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        """  
        x: Tensor of shape (batch, seq\_len, in\_channels)  
        mask: Tensor of shape (batch, seq\_len) with 1 for valid, 0 for missing  
        """  
        \# Zero-out the masked timesteps to prevent contamination during convolution  
        mask\_expanded \= mask.unsqueeze(-1)  
        x \= x \* mask\_expanded  
          
        \# Rearrange for Conv1d expectation: (batch, channels, seq\_len)  
        x \= x.transpose(1, 2)  
          
        \# Convolutional Block 1  
        x \= F.relu(self.bn1(self.conv1(x)))  
        x \= self.dropout(x)  
          
        \# Convolutional Block 2  
        x \= F.relu(self.bn2(self.conv2(x)))  
        x \= self.dropout(x)  
          
        \# Convolutional Block 3  
        x \= F.relu(self.bn3(self.conv3(x)))  
          
        \# Masked Global Average Pooling over the temporal axis  
        mask\_pool \= mask.unsqueeze(1)  
        sum\_features \= torch.sum(x \* mask\_pool, dim=2)  
        valid\_counts \= torch.clamp(torch.sum(mask\_pool, dim=2), min\=1.0)  
          
        pooled\_features \= sum\_features / valid\_counts  
          
        \# Final projection to invariant d\_model space  
        out \= self.fc(pooled\_features)  
        return out

## **VI. Domain Physics and Capacity-Neutral Feature Reframing**

Appending raw spectral indices directly to the sequence channels has empirically destroyed baseline performance by overloading the network capacity with redundant, highly collinear variables. A fundamentally superior approach reframes the input space through hard-coded physical decision boundaries before passing the resulting low-dimensional vector into the neural network's projection layer43.

### **The Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 Monsoon Asymmetry**

During the monsoon season, massive optical masking occurs. The active Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) of Sentinel-1 operates in the C-band (\~5.4 GHz) and transmits its own microwave energy, allowing it to natively penetrate cloud cover and precipitation46. Consequently, S1 sequences maintain physical integrity where Sentinel-2 sequences fail.  
Rather than allowing the network to struggle with cross-sensor data imputation, the pipeline must strictly decouple the optical and radar feature extraction spaces44.

* **Sentinel-1 Radar Extraction**: Extracted exclusively as statistical percentiles (![][image34], ![][image35], ![][image36]) evaluated specifically over the non-masked radar months. Because active C-band radar experiences specular reflection (where energy bounces away from the sensor) when hitting calm standing water, a persistent low ![][image34] percentile backscatter is the strongest single physical indicator of a managed pond46.

### **The Zou et al. (2018) Multi-Index Water Tree**

Over the valid Sentinel-2 optical months, a sequence of robust water indices can reliably filter urban backgrounds, shadow artifacts, and vegetative cover. The relevant indices utilized in the Zou framework rely on distinct Sentinel-2 multispectral wavelengths43:

| Spectral Index | Wavelengths Utilized (Sentinel-2) | Primary Function in Water Detection |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **MNDWI** | Green (B3), SWIR1 (B11) | Replaces NIR with SWIR to suppress built-up land noise48. |
| **NDVI** | NIR (B8), Red (B4) | Differentiates vegetation from open water49. |
| **EVI** | NIR (B8), Red (B4), Blue (B2) | Enhances vegetation signal in high biomass regions to prevent false positives45. |
| **AWEI\_nsh** | Green (B3), NIR (B8), SWIR1 (B11), SWIR2 (B12) | Excludes urban background interference in areas with minimal shadow49. |
| **AWEI\_sh** | Blue (B2), Green (B3), NIR (B8), SWIR1, SWIR2 | Explicitly designed to eliminate terrain and cloud shadow pixels43. |

The exact index formulas applied to the Sentinel-2 bands are defined as:  
![][image37]  
![][image38]  
![][image39]  
![][image40]  
The Zou et al. Multi-Index Water Tree evaluates a hierarchical boolean logic sequence for every valid timestep ![][image41]43:  
![][image42]  
This formulation translates the raw 10-band optical sequence into a rigid physical invariant binary mapping45. The boolean sequence is then temporally pooled into a Water Inundation Frequency (WIF) representation, capturing the persistence of surface water required to classify managed aquaculture against temporary flooding.

### **PyTorch Implementation: Physics Feature Reframing**

This implementation calculates the decoupled invariants in a mathematically safe, vectorized format, strictly shielding the tensor operations from the \-9999 placeholders.

Python  
import torch

class PhysicsInvariantExtractor:  
    """  
    Decouples S1 and S2 sequences, safely bypasses \-9999 masked values,   
    and applies the Zou et al. Multi-Index Water Tree to project the sequence  
    into a low-dimensional physical space.  
    """  
    def \_\_init\_\_(self, band\_indices: dict):  
        \# Dictionary mapping string band names to their integer channel index  
        self.idx \= band\_indices 

    def extract\_invariants(self, sequence: torch.Tensor) \-\> torch.Tensor:  
        """  
        Args:  
            sequence: Tensor of shape (batch, seq\_len, num\_bands)  
        Returns:   
            invariants: Tensor of shape (batch, 4\) representing   
                        \[WIF, Max\_Water, VV\_10th, S2\_Valid\_Ratio\]  
        """  
        batch\_size, seq\_len, \_ \= sequence.shape  
        device \= sequence.device  
          
        \# \--- Sentinel-1 Radar Processing \---  
        vv \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['VV'\]\]  
        vh \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['VH'\]\]  
          
        \# Valid S1 mask (radar penetrates clouds, check for absolute padding)  
        s1\_mask \= (vv \!= \-9999) & (vh \!= \-9999)  
          
        \# Calculate 10th percentile over valid S1 backscatter safely  
        \# Fill masked with a high positive value to ignore in lower percentile calculation  
        vv\_safe \= torch.where(s1\_mask, vv, torch.tensor(999.0, device=device))  
        vv\_10th \= torch.quantile(vv\_safe, 0.10, dim=1, keepdim=True)  
          
        \# If a row was entirely missing, reset to 0 to prevent NaN propagation  
        s1\_row\_mask \= s1\_mask.any(dim=1, keepdim=True)  
        vv\_10th \= torch.where(s1\_row\_mask, vv\_10th, torch.tensor(0.0, device=device))  
          
        \# \--- Sentinel-2 Optical Processing \---  
        green \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['Green'\]\]  
        red \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['Red'\]\]  
        blue \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['Blue'\]\]  
        nir \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['NIR'\]\]  
        swir1 \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['SWIR1'\]\]  
        swir2 \= sequence\[:, :, self.idx\['SWIR2'\]\]  
          
        \# Valid S2 mask (filters monsoon dropouts)  
        s2\_mask \= (green \!= \-9999) & (swir1 \!= \-9999)  
          
        \# Safe addition constant to prevent divide-by-zero during masking  
        eps \= 1e-6  
          
        mndwi \= (green \- swir1) / (green \+ swir1 \+ eps)  
        ndvi \= (nir \- red) / (nir \+ red \+ eps)  
        evi \= 2.5 \* (nir \- red) / (nir \+ 6.0 \* red \- 7.5 \* blue \+ 1.0 \+ eps)  
          
        awei\_nsh \= 4.0 \* (green \- swir1) \- (0.25 \* nir \+ 2.75 \* swir2)  
        awei\_sh \= blue \+ 2.5 \* green \- 1.5 \* (nir \+ swir1) \- 0.25 \* swir2  
          
        \# Zou et al. Water Tree Logic evaluation  
        cond1 \= (mndwi \> evi) | (mndwi \> ndvi)  
        cond2 \= evi \< 0.1  
        cond3 \= (awei\_nsh \> 0) | (awei\_sh \> \-0.1)  
          
        is\_water \= cond1 & cond2 & cond3  
          
        \# Apply the physical S2 mask (only valid if optical data was present)  
        is\_water \= is\_water & s2\_mask  
          
        \# Calculate Water Inundation Frequency (WIF)  
        valid\_s2\_counts \= torch.clamp(torch.sum(s2\_mask, dim=1, keepdim=True), min\=1.0)  
        wif \= torch.sum(is\_water, dim=1, keepdim=True) / valid\_s2\_counts  
          
        \# If no valid optical data existed in the row, set WIF to 0  
        s2\_row\_mask \= s2\_mask.any(dim=1, keepdim=True)  
        wif \= torch.where(s2\_row\_mask, wif, torch.tensor(0.0, device=device))  
          
        \# Extract maximum presence indicating at least one clear water observation  
        water\_max \= torch.max(is\_water.float(), dim=1, keepdim=True)\[0\]  
          
        \# Combine invariants into a 4-dimensional vector  
        s2\_valid\_ratio \= valid\_s2\_counts / seq\_len  
        invariants \= torch.cat(\[wif, water\_max, vv\_10th, s2\_valid\_ratio\], dim=1)  
          
        return invariants

By concatenating this isolated 4-dimensional invariant vector to the Transformer's linear projection output, the architecture receives heavily compressed, deterministic physical states that remain unaffected by absolute radiometric shifts, completely bypassing the catastrophic parameter-bloating associated with appending sequence channels.

## **VII. Strategic Synthesis**

The challenge of aquaculture pond detection inside a globally misaligned dataset necessitates a radical departure from conventional deep sequence modeling. The presence of adversarial masking, monsoon-induced sensor dropouts, and rigid classification thresholds render high-capacity, uncalibrated networks effectively obsolete. To achieve a Top-5 standing (0.945+) on the final leaderboard, the engineering pipeline must execute the following integrated sequence:

> 1. Replace the rigid absolute temporal positional encodings with the **Set Transformer (ISAB/PMA)** formulation, rendering the network immune to the sequence padding variance caused by variable 4-6 month masking blocks29.  
> 2. Deploy the **CropNet Temporal Backbone** as a parallel ensemble regularizer. Its narrow, temporal-first convolutional receptive field acts as a high-bias anchor against the high-variance tendency of the Set Transformer, capturing localized invariant state transitions26.  
> 3. Implement the **Zou et al. Multi-Index Water Tree** as a capacity-neutral physical feature gate. This entirely isolates the stable C-band S1 backscatter from the volatile, monsoon-corrupted S2 optical sequences, feeding the network incontrovertible physical invariants without bloating channel dimensions43.  
> 4. Align the latent covariance spaces during training using the **Deep CORAL loss**, and perform **TENT-based Test-Time Adaptation** during inference to optimize the projection weights against the unlabelled target domain7.  
> 5. Calibrate the raw predictive logits using the **Saerens Expectation-Maximization (MLLS)** algorithm before the final sigmoid activation, mathematically guaranteeing that the predicted posterior perfectly mirrors the shifted target prior under the rigid 0.5 evaluation threshold1.
